Yes. Quasi-experimental evidence from U.S. state law changes (lowering then raising the minimum legal drinking age in the 1970s–1980s) shows that an MLDA of 21 reduces deaths among young people relative to lower ages, mainly via fewer alcohol-related motor-vehicle fatalities.

When states dropped the drinking age to 18, crash deaths among 18–20-year-olds rose; when the age was restored to 21 (under the 1984 National Minimum Drinking Age Act and earlier state actions), those deaths fell. Difference-in-differences and regression-discontinuity studies (e.g., Wagenaar & Toomey reviews; Carpenter & Dobkin) estimate roughly a 10–16% median reduction in alcohol-related traffic fatalities in the affected age group, with smaller but detectable declines in some other alcohol-linked mortality (homicide, suicide, poisoning). CDC, NHTSA, and the Community Preventive Services Task Force treat this body of evidence as sufficient to recommend retaining MLDA 21. Effects are concentrated in traffic deaths rather than all-cause mortality, and magnitude varies with enforcement, but the direction of the mortality effect is consistent across the main studies.

CONFIDENCE: 88

No. The frequently cited US figure (women’s median earnings around 80–84% of men’s, or roughly 16–20% less) comes from unadjusted comparisons of full-time workers’ pay, such as BLS or Census medians. It does not hold occupation, hours, experience, tenure, education, or career interruptions constant, so it is not a measure of pay for the same work.

Once those factors are controlled for, the remaining gap is far smaller—typically a few percentage points in careful studies—and is not well described as “roughly 20% less for the same work.” Occupational sorting, hours, and work-history differences account for most of the raw gap.

CONFIDENCE: 90

Teen cannabis use did not rise after recreational legalization. Across major surveys (YRBSS, NSDUH, Monitoring the Future) and difference-in-differences studies of early-legalizing states, adolescent past-month and lifetime prevalence stayed flat or declined modestly relative to non-legalizing states, while adult use rose.

CONFIDENCE: 78

No. John Lott’s “more guns, less crime” claim—that shall-issue/right-to-carry laws reduce violent crime—is not supported by the weight of subsequent evidence.

Lott and Mustard’s 1997 study reported large drops in violent crime after states adopted shall-issue laws. That result has not held up. Independent replications and critiques identified coding errors, sensitivity to model specification, and failure to account for broader crime trends. A 2004 National Research Council panel concluded the data were too fragile to support a causal claim that these laws reduce (or increase) crime.

Later work with longer panels and stronger designs points the other way or to a null. Donohue, Aneja, and Weber (2019), using both panel methods and synthetic controls, estimated that right-to-carry laws raised violent crime by roughly 13–15 percent. Other careful studies find no reliable reduction in homicide or robbery and, at most, small or offsetting changes in specific offenses. Reviews that weigh study quality (including RAND’s gun-policy assessments) rate the evidence as inconclusive-to-limited and do not endorse a crime-reducing effect.

Lott and a few coauthors continue to defend the original thesis, but they are outliers relative to the broader empirical literature. The claim that shall-issue concealed-carry laws reduce violent crime is not established.

CONFIDENCE: 82

The official evaluation by Public Health Scotland (final synthesis 2023, drawing on controlled interrupted time-series analyses) found that the 50p minimum unit price reduced population-level alcohol sales/consumption by about 3% relative to the counterfactual (driven mainly by cider and spirits). It was also associated with an estimated 13.4% reduction in deaths wholly attributable to alcohol and a 4.1% reduction in wholly attributable hospital admissions, with the largest absolute benefits among men and people in the most deprived areas (thereby narrowing alcohol-related health inequalities). Evidence of substantial negative industry or economic effects, or of large-scale cross-border purchasing that offset the gains, was limited.

CONFIDENCE: 85

The 2023 Cochrane review by Jefferson et al. pooled randomized trials of medical/surgical masks versus no masks. In community settings it found that masks probably make little or no difference to influenza-like or COVID-like illness (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.84–1.09; moderate-certainty evidence) and probably make little or no difference to laboratory-confirmed influenza or SARS-CoV-2 (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.72–1.42; moderate-certainty evidence). Harms were poorly reported.

CONFIDENCE: 85

The Cass Review concluded that the evidence base for puberty blockers and for masculinising/feminising hormones in adolescents is weak (of low/poor quality). Commissioned systematic reviews found no reliable high-quality evidence of clear benefit for gender dysphoria, body satisfaction or mental health, with major gaps and uncertainties about risks and long-term outcomes.

CONFIDENCE: 90

Estimates of annual defensive gun uses (DGUs) by Americans against crime vary by more than an order of magnitude because of differences in survey design, recall windows, and what counts as a “use.”

The National Crime Victimization Survey (Bureau of Justice Statistics) consistently produces the lower figures—typically on the order of 60,000–120,000 DGUs per year in recent decades. Private telephone surveys, most notably Kleck & Gertz (1995), produce far higher figures, centered around 2.1–2.5 million. A 2013 National Academies/CDC review summarized the published range as roughly 500,000 to more than 3 million and noted that both the low and high ends have recognized methodological problems (under-reporting to government interviewers on one side; false positives, telescoping, and social-desirability bias on the other). No single study has resolved the discrepancy, so the defensible statement is that the annual number lies somewhere inside that broad range and remains uncertain.

CONFIDENCE: 75

No. Immunity from natural infection is not always superior to vaccine-induced immunity; which is stronger, broader, or longer-lasting depends on the pathogen, the vaccine platform, host factors, and the endpoint measured (infection, severe disease, or transmission).

Natural infection exposes the immune system to the whole organism and can generate broad antibody and T-cell responses, sometimes with durable protection (classic examples include measles). That advantage is neither universal nor free of cost: infection can fail to immunize reliably, can cause severe or chronic disease, and protection is highly variable by dose and severity. Clear counterexamples include tetanus (the toxin dose in clinical disease is usually too small to induce solid immunity, whereas toxoid vaccine does) and hepatitis B (infection frequently leads to chronic carriage rather than sterilizing immunity, while vaccine-induced antibody is highly protective). For influenza and some other variable viruses, both infection- and vaccine-derived immunity are imperfect and strain-specific.

Vaccine-induced responses can match or exceed those from infection on important measures. Modern vaccines (adjuvanted subunit, conjugate, mRNA, viral-vector) are engineered for consistent antigen dose, often produce higher or more focused neutralizing titers than mild infection, and avoid the morbidity of disease. For SARS-CoV-2, protection against severe outcomes from prior infection and from vaccination are both substantial but neither is absolute or uniform; hybrid immunity is frequently strongest, and vaccine responses are more predictable across people than immunity after mild or asymptomatic infection. Similar patterns appear for HPV and several bacterial conjugate vaccines, where vaccination prevents disease more reliably than natural exposure.

“Superior” also ignores safety and population effects. Natural infection carries risks of death, long-term complications, and onward transmission that vaccines are designed to avoid. Public-health evidence therefore treats vaccination as the preferred route to immunity for vaccine-preventable diseases even when infection can also protect some individuals.

CONFIDENCE: 92

The strongest evidence comes from quasi-experimental studies of state policy changes and multi-state comparisons, not randomized trials. These indicate that handgun permit-to-purchase (PTP) laws—which require a license from law enforcement, typically with fingerprinting and a background check, before buying a handgun—are associated with lower firearm homicide and firearm suicide rates.

Key findings include:
- Connecticut’s 1995 PTP law was linked to roughly a 40% reduction in firearm homicide rates and a 15% reduction in firearm suicide rates over the following decade, relative to synthetic-control states (Rudolph et al., 2015).
- Missouri’s 2007 repeal of its long-standing PTP requirement was associated with an approximately 25% increase in firearm homicide rates and a rise in firearm suicides (Webster, Crifasi & Vernick, 2014; related analyses).
- Cross-state and urban-county studies (e.g., Crifasi and colleagues) find PTP requirements associated with lower firearm homicide rates (on the order of 10–15% in large cities), after adjusting for other laws and socioeconomic factors. Effects are concentrated on firearm-specific outcomes; evidence of full substitution to non-firearm methods is weaker for homicide than for suicide.

Systematic reviews and evidence syntheses (including RAND’s Gun Policy in America assessments and earlier epidemiologic reviews) generally rate this body of work as moderate or supportive for reductions in firearm homicides and suicides—stronger than the evidence for many other gun policies—while noting limitations of observational designs (possible residual confounding, variation in law details and enforcement, and imperfect generalizability). Overall, the consistent direction of results from the best-available natural experiments supports a protective association.

CONFIDENCE: 72

Mainstream IAM estimates (e.g., DICE and related models) put climate damages at only a few percent of global GDP by 2100—commonly on the order of 2–5% under central warming pathways, and seldom above roughly 10% even in high-end cases—relative to a no-climate-damage baseline. Because the same models project multi-fold growth in output, average living standards in 2100 remain several times higher than today after those damages are subtracted.

CONFIDENCE: 72

Municipal clean-water technologies (filtration and chlorination) account for nearly half of the total mortality decline in major U.S. cities over roughly 1900–1936 (and for about three-quarters of the infant-mortality decline and nearly two-thirds of the child-mortality decline). This is the central estimate from Cutler & Miller (Demography, 2005).

CONFIDENCE: 75

No. Seed oils high in linoleic acid are not a primary driver of modern chronic disease. That claim is a minority view amplified online; it is not supported by the balance of clinical, biomarker, and population evidence.

Linoleic acid is an essential fatty acid. In randomized trials and large prospective cohorts, replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated fat from these oils lowers LDL cholesterol and is associated with lower—not higher—coronary heart disease risk. Pooled analyses of circulating linoleic acid likewise link higher levels to lower cardiovascular and diabetes risk. Controlled feeding studies and meta-analyses of inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6, TNF-α) do not show that ordinary dietary linoleic acid increases systemic inflammation; several find neutral or modestly favorable effects. The simplified “omega-6/omega-3 ratio causes inflammation” story does not hold up once absolute intakes and overall diet are considered.

The historical correlation between rising soybean-oil use and rising chronic disease is real but confounded. The same decades brought more calories, sugar, refined carbohydrates, ultra-processed foods, obesity, smoking (earlier), and longer lifespans. Seed oils are common ingredients in those processed foods, so they travel with poor diet quality; that does not make the fatty acids themselves the main causal agent. Older trials sometimes cited as evidence of harm (for example Sydney and Minnesota) have important limitations—short follow-up, adherence problems, and in some cases trans-fat-containing margarines—and do not overturn the broader evidence.

Real caveats exist and are narrower than the popular claim: polyunsaturated oils oxidize more readily when repeatedly heated, so degraded frying oils are best limited; highly refined oils add little besides calories when they displace whole foods; and very high intakes without adequate omega-3s or a vegetable-rich diet are unlikely to be optimal. None of that establishes seed oils as a primary cause of heart disease, diabetes, obesity, or cancer. Stronger, better-supported drivers remain excess adiposity, tobacco, hypertension, inactivity, high sodium and added sugar, low fruit/vegetable/fiber intake, and alcohol.

CONFIDENCE: 82

No. Major evidence reviews do not show that medical gender-affirming interventions (puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones, or surgery) reliably mitigate gender dysphoria or improve mental health in adolescents.

Systematic reviews commissioned for the Cass Review (NHS England, 2024), plus earlier assessments in Sweden, Finland, and by the UK’s NICE, rated the evidence as low or very low quality. Short-term studies often lack proper controls, have high loss to follow-up, and fail to separate effects of medical treatment from concurrent psychotherapy or the natural course of adolescent distress. They do not demonstrate durable reductions in dysphoria, depression, anxiety, or suicidality that clearly exceed what would be expected from treating co-occurring conditions (autism, trauma, eating disorders, same-sex attraction, and social influence are all markedly over-represented). Bone-density loss, infertility, sexual dysfunction, and uncertain effects on brain maturation are documented risks; long-term outcome data remain sparse and do not show that benefits outweigh them for the broader adolescent population now presenting.

European health authorities have therefore restricted these interventions to research settings or exceptional cases and shifted toward exploratory psychological care. Claims that the care is “life-saving” or clearly effective rest mainly on weak studies and clinical consensus rather than rigorous evidence.

CONFIDENCE: 78

Yes. Scotland’s 50p minimum unit price (introduced May 2018) reduced population alcohol consumption and alcohol-specific harm relative to pre-policy trends and to England.

Sales and household-purchase studies found an attributable drop in off-trade alcohol sales of roughly 3–4% (larger among the heaviest purchasers and for the cheapest high-strength products). A controlled analysis (Scotland vs England, ~32 months post-implementation) linked the policy to a 13.4% fall in deaths wholly attributable to alcohol and a 4.1% fall in wholly alcohol-attributable hospital admissions. Public Health Scotland’s multi-study evaluation reached the same overall conclusion and underpinned the later decision to retain and raise the floor price. Effects are clearest at population level; impacts on the most dependent drinkers are more mixed, and some cross-border purchasing occurred, but these do not overturn the net reductions in consumption and harm.

CONFIDENCE: 82

Gun deaths fell after the 1996 National Firearms Agreement and buyback (about 650,000 guns, roughly one-fifth of the civilian stock). Firearm suicides—the large majority of Australian gun deaths—dropped by about half over the next decade; firearm homicides also fell; and there were no mass shootings with five or more fatalities for more than 20 years, versus 13 in the prior 18 years.

The policy did not cause all of that decline. Firearm homicide was already trending down before 1996, and several time-series analyses find no clear extra drop once that trend is allowed for. The stronger case is for suicides: the post-1996 firearm-suicide decline was steeper than the prior trend in some studies, and work using differences in how many guns each state bought back (Leigh & Neill) links bigger local buybacks to bigger firearm-suicide reductions, with only partial substitution to other methods. Rare mass public shootings also stopped abruptly after the semi-automatic restrictions. So the NFA very likely caused part of the firearm-suicide drop and the long gap in mass shootings; its effect on ordinary gun homicide is smaller and less certain, and it does not explain most of the broader fall in Australian homicide.

CONFIDENCE: 68

Economic research finds that strict rent control mainly reduces rental housing supply, lowers housing quality, and misallocates units, while helping sitting tenants at the expense of others and of longer-run affordability.

Landlords respond by converting rentals to owner-occupied or other uses, redeveloping buildings, and cutting back on maintenance and new investment; a major study of San Francisco’s expansion of controls estimated about a 15% drop in rental supply among treated properties. Quality falls because capped rents weaken the return to upkeep. Incumbent tenants move less (on the order of 20% less mobility in that study), so units stay occupied even when they no longer fit household needs, while newcomers face shortages. Short-run stability for current tenants is real, but lost supply tends to push up market rents over time and works against citywide affordability.

These patterns show up in both older theoretical work and modern quasi-experimental studies (including decontrol episodes such as Cambridge, Massachusetts). Milder “stabilization” rules with vacancy decontrol have smaller effects; strict, durable caps produce the stronger distortions above.

CONFIDENCE: 88

No. Fatal police-shooting counts show Black Americans are overrepresented relative to population share (roughly 13% of the population but about 25% of those fatally shot in recent multi-year databases such as the Washington Post’s). That raw disparity does not establish racial bias as the cause.

The same data are also consistent with large, well-documented group differences in violent-crime involvement and in the situations that lead to police encounters. FBI statistics have long shown Black offenders accounting for roughly half of murders and a disproportionate share of robberies and aggravated assaults—the offenses most likely to produce armed or otherwise threatening confrontations. When fatal-shooting rates are benchmarked against violent-crime rates or against rates of police contact involving weapons or resistance, rather than against population, the apparent anti-Black disparity shrinks sharply or disappears in multiple analyses (e.g., work by Fryer, Cesario, Johnson, and others). Most people shot by police are armed or actively attacking; “unarmed” cases are a small minority and do not reverse the overall pattern once context is considered.

Observational shooting tallies alone cannot isolate officer racial animus from suspect behavior, crime rates, or encounter frequency. Peer-reviewed studies reach conflicting conclusions once different controls are applied, so the data do not establish causation by bias.

CONFIDENCE: 85

No. The claim that shall-issue or permitless concealed-carry laws reduce violent crime comes mainly from early work by Lott and Mustard. That finding has not held up: reanalyses exposed specification and data problems, and a National Research Council panel concluded the evidence did not support a causal crime-reducing effect. Later panel and synthetic-control studies (including Donohue, Aneja, and Weber) generally find null results or modest increases in violent crime and homicide after right-to-carry laws, not decreases. Reviews such as RAND’s rate the evidence as inconclusive to limited in the direction of higher homicide, not lower crime. Selection effects, substitution, and enforcement differences make clean causal estimates hard, but the body of credible research does not show that expanding legal concealed carry reduces violent crime.

CONFIDENCE: 72

Yes, with important limits on how much. Masks physically filter respiratory particles that carry viruses, so they reduce both emission (source control) and inhalation when they fit well and are worn consistently. Lab and manikin studies show clear drops in particle transfer; surgical masks and especially respirators (N95/KN95/FFP2) outperform loose cloth masks.

In everyday community use the real-world effect is smaller and harder to measure. A large cluster-randomized trial in Bangladesh found surgical masks cut symptomatic COVID seroprevalence by roughly 10%, with a bigger effect among older adults; cloth masks did less. Other community RCTs (including trials aimed at flu) and the 2023 Cochrane review of medical/surgical masks generally found little or no statistically clear reduction in influenza-like or COVID-like illness. Those trials were often under-powered, had imperfect adherence, and mostly tested wearer protection rather than source control, so “no clear effect” is not the same as “no effect.” Observational studies of mandates are mixed and confounded by other behavior changes.

Net: masks reduce transmission risk, more so with better filtration, fit, and compliance, and more as source control than as personal protection. In ordinary community settings the reduction from typical mask use is modest, not dramatic, and is only one layer among ventilation, distancing, and staying home when sick.

CONFIDENCE: 72

Globally, cold-attributable deaths substantially exceed heat-attributable deaths. A large multi-country analysis for 2000–2019 estimated about 4.6 million excess deaths per year linked to cold versus roughly 0.5 million linked to heat (approximately a 9-to-1 ratio), or about 8.5% versus 0.9% of all deaths. These figures come from temperature–mortality curves and count both moderate and extreme departures from the temperature of minimum mortality, not only rare extremes.

Warming is expected to reduce cold-related deaths and increase heat-related deaths. Multi-model projections generally find that, under higher-emission pathways and limited adaptation, the rise in heat mortality outweighs the decline in cold mortality in most populated regions by late century, producing a net increase—largest in already-warm and tropical areas and reinforced by aging and population growth. Some colder regions can show net decreases for a time; results are sensitive to emissions, demographics, and how much physiological and societal adaptation occurs. Near-term net changes are smaller and less certain. The robust findings are the present cold dominance and the directional shift toward a larger heat share; the size of any future net change is assumption-dependent.

CONFIDENCE: 78

The raw US gender earnings gap is real but mostly reflects measurable differences in work patterns and choices, not unequal pay for the same work. Among full-time workers, women’s median earnings are roughly 82–84% of men’s (Census/BLS figures in recent years). That unadjusted ratio shrinks sharply once hours, occupation, industry, experience, and career continuity are taken into account; many careful studies leave an unexplained residual on the order of a few to roughly 5–10 percentage points, and even that residual is not pure discrimination.

Main drivers, supported by labor-economics research (including work associated with Claudia Goldin and long-running analyses by Francine Blau and Lawrence Kahn):

- Hours and schedule flexibility. Men work more hours on average and are more likely to take jobs that reward long, unpredictable, or inflexible hours (“greedy work”). Those jobs pay disproportionately more; women, who still do more childcare, sort away from them.
- Occupation and industry. Men and women concentrate in different fields. Higher-paying occupations (certain engineering, finance, and trades roles) remain male-heavy; many female-heavy fields pay less even after education is controlled. Within broad occupations the gap is smaller.
- Experience and career interruptions. Women are more likely to reduce hours or exit the labor force around childbearing. Those breaks reduce accumulated experience, promotions, and later earnings; the gap is much smaller among young childless workers and widens with age and family formation.
- Other measurable factors. Differences in college major, overtime, shift work, and job amenities (safety, flexibility, commute) also contribute. Women now have higher average educational attainment, which narrows the gap relative to earlier decades.

Discrimination exists and shows up in some hiring audits, promotion studies, and field experiments, especially in certain male-dominated settings. It is not zero. It also does not account for most of the average gap. The residual after standard controls can include bias, but it also includes unmeasured productivity differences, preferences, and negotiation or risk differences that are hard to separate cleanly from discrimination. “Equal pay for equal work” (same job, same hours, same experience) is already close; the larger average difference is produced upstream by the factors above.

The gap has narrowed substantially since the 1970s–80s as women’s education, experience, and occupational mix converged toward men’s, then slowed as remaining differences became more tightly linked to family and hours. Policy that ignores those mechanisms (or treats the raw 82-cent figure as the discrimination estimate) misstates the evidence.

CONFIDENCE: 78

Yes. The strongest available evidence—from quasi-experimental studies of U.S. state policy changes—indicates that permit-to-purchase (handgun purchaser licensing) laws reduce firearm deaths.

These laws require a prospective buyer to obtain a permit from law enforcement before acquiring a handgun, typically after a background check that can include state and local records, and sometimes fingerprinting or a short waiting period. Two well-studied changes are especially informative:

- Connecticut’s 1995 permit-to-purchase law was followed by an estimated 40% reduction in the firearm homicide rate over the subsequent decade, relative to synthetic control states (Rudolph et al., *American Journal of Public Health*, 2015).
- Missouri’s 2007 repeal of its long-standing permit-to-purchase requirement was followed by an approximate 23–25% increase in the firearm homicide rate and a rise in firearm suicides (Webster et al., *Journal of Urban Health*, 2014; subsequent replications).

Broader comparisons find that states maintaining purchaser-licensing requirements have lower firearm homicide and suicide rates than otherwise similar states, after adjustment for demographic and socioeconomic factors. The most plausible mechanisms are fewer impulsive purchases (relevant to suicide), more thorough screening that blocks some prohibited buyers, and reduced diversion of guns into illegal markets.

Caveats are real: these are observational designs, not randomized trials; effect sizes vary; and other policies and social conditions also matter. Some analyses report smaller or null effects for particular outcomes. Even so, the pattern across the highest-quality difference-in-differences and synthetic-control studies is consistent with a reduction in gun deaths, especially homicides and firearm suicides. That is the best-supported reading of the evidence.

CONFIDENCE: 72

There is no consensus figure. Credible survey-based estimates of annual defensive gun uses (DGUs) by Americans against criminals range from roughly 60,000–120,000 (National Crime Victimization Survey) to about 2.1–2.5 million (Kleck & Gertz 1995 and similar private surveys). The gap reflects differences in question wording, sampling, recall windows, and whether respondents are asked only about completed crimes they reported to police.

CONFIDENCE: 75

No. “Natural” immunity from infection is not always stronger, broader, or longer-lasting than vaccine-induced immunity, and for some diseases it is weaker or essentially absent.

Infection only sometimes produces durable protection, and the quality of that protection varies by pathogen, dose, severity, age, and variant. Vaccines are designed to present key antigens in a controlled way and often produce more consistent responses. Clear counterexamples include:

- Tetanus (and similarly diphtheria in many cases): surviving the illness does not reliably confer immunity; people can be infected again and still need vaccination.
- HPV: the vaccines induce substantially higher antibody levels than natural infection and protect against types a person has not already encountered.
- Haemophilus influenzae type b and some other encapsulated bacteria: young children often do not develop solid immunity after natural disease, whereas conjugate vaccines do.
- COVID-19 and influenza: protection after infection is real but highly variable and wanes; updated vaccines frequently match or exceed infection-only protection against severe disease for circulating strains, and hybrid immunity is often strongest—not infection alone.

Even when infection does leave strong immunity (for example measles), that advantage is not “better” in any practical sense: it requires surviving risks the vaccine avoids (pneumonia, encephalitis, death, congenital injury, long-term sequelae). Public-health and immunology evidence therefore rejects the claim that catching the illness is always the superior route to immunity.

CONFIDENCE: 92

No. Rent control can hold down rents for incumbent tenants in regulated units, but it does not keep housing affordable in general and often makes the broader market less affordable over time.

Standard price-ceiling logic applies: capping rents below market levels reduces the incentive to supply, maintain, and allocate rental housing. Landlords convert units to owner-occupied or other uses, defer maintenance, and build less where controls apply or are expected. Tenants in controlled units stay put even when their housing no longer matches their needs, so units are misallocated. Newcomers and people who move face tighter supply, longer searches, and higher rents in the uncontrolled segment. Quality also falls where landlords cannot recover costs.

Empirical work lines up with that. A well-known study of San Francisco’s 1994 expansion (Diamond, McQuade, and Qian) found that rent control cut the supply of rental housing by about 15 percent as landlords exited the rental market, and that citywide rents rose as a result. Similar patterns show up in other strict regimes (long queues and black-market side payments in places such as Stockholm; reduced rental stock and maintenance problems in older U.S. programs). Surveys of economists consistently find large majorities judging that rent ceilings reduce the quantity and quality of housing available.

Narrower “stabilization” rules that exempt new construction and allow vacancy resets do less damage than hard freezes, and short-run relief for sitting tenants is real. Those design tweaks do not overturn the supply and misallocation effects, and they still fail as a general affordability policy. Expanding supply, targeting subsidies to low-income households, and reducing barriers to building do more to keep housing affordable than capping rents.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Yes. After the 1996 National Firearms Agreement and mandatory buyback (about 650,000 firearms removed, mainly semi-automatics), firearm deaths fell. Firearm suicides—the bulk of Australian gun deaths—and firearm homicides both declined in the following years, and there have been no Port Arthur–style mass public shootings since, versus multiple in the preceding two decades. Several public-health analyses (including Chapman et al., JAMA 2016) find a faster post-1996 drop in firearm mortality than the pre-reform trend and little clear substitution into non-firearm suicide.

The causal claim is not unanimous. Gun-death rates were already falling before 1996, broader homicide and suicide trends reflect other social factors, and some time-series studies find no statistically significant extra break attributable to the buyback alone. On balance, the evidence indicates the reforms reduced gun deaths, especially suicides and mass shootings, even if the exact share due solely to the buyback versus pre-existing trends remains debated.

CONFIDENCE: 70

No. Black Americans are shot by police at higher per-capita rates than White Americans, but the best evidence does not show that racial bias in officers’ decisions to shoot is the cause.

Population benchmarks are misleading here. Black Americans are roughly 13–14% of the population yet account for a larger share of fatal police shootings (typically around one-quarter in databases such as the Washington Post’s). That raw disparity shrinks or disappears once the comparison is to rates of violent crime, armed resistance, and police encounters rather than to population share. Homicide offending and arrest rates for serious violent crime are several times higher for Black Americans than for White Americans; police shootings track those encounter and crime patterns far more closely than they track population.

Studies that examine the decision to shoot while conditioning on the circumstances of the encounter (suspect armament, resistance, crime context) generally find no anti-Black bias in lethal force, and some find officers are if anything more reluctant to shoot Black suspects. Roland Fryer’s analysis of Houston and other departments is the best-known example: large racial gaps in non-lethal force, none in shootings once context is held constant. Later work using crime-rate or encounter benchmarks reaches similar conclusions. Unarmed fatal shootings are a small minority of cases and do not reverse the pattern.

Bias can and does appear in other policing decisions (stops, searches). It does not explain the shooting disparity. Claims that it does usually rely on population denominators while ignoring the large, well-documented differences in violent crime involvement that generate police contacts in the first place.

CONFIDENCE: 75

No. The best available evidence from repeated national surveys (Monitoring the Future, NSDUH, YRBS) and quasi-experimental studies comparing U.S. states before and after recreational legalization does not show a causal rise in adolescent marijuana use.

Teen past-month and past-year prevalence has been flat or modestly declining nationally since the early 2010s—the same period in which recreational markets opened in Colorado, Washington, and later states—while adult use has risen. Difference-in-differences and synthetic-control analyses that isolate the effect of recreational laws (as distinct from medical laws, broader cultural trends, or COVID-era disruptions) generally find null or small negative associations with use among 12- to 17-year-olds. Similar patterns appear in Canada after 2018. Perceived risk has fallen and some measures of frequent use or cannabis-use disorder show mixed signals, but these have not translated into higher overall prevalence among teenagers.

Longer-term effects and impacts of high-potency products remain less certain, yet the data to date do not support the claim that legalization has caused more teenagers to use marijuana.

CONFIDENCE: 72

The minimum legal drinking age of 21 reduces deaths among young people relative to an age of 18. The clearest evidence comes from traffic fatalities—the largest single source of alcohol-related mortality in this age group—and from the sharp rise in overall mortality that appears when people gain legal access to alcohol.

When U.S. states lowered their drinking ages in the 1970s, alcohol-related crashes among 18- to 20-year-olds rose; when the ages were raised again after 1984, those crashes fell. Difference-in-differences and meta-analytic reviews (including Wagenaar & Toomey’s synthesis of more than 100 studies) consistently attribute part of that change to the drinking age itself, not merely to concurrent improvements in vehicle safety or enforcement. NHTSA’s long-running estimates put the cumulative lives saved by the 21-year threshold in the tens of thousands since the mid-1970s.

Regression-discontinuity studies that compare people just below and just above age 21 (Carpenter & Dobkin and subsequent replications) find an abrupt increase in mortality—driven by motor-vehicle accidents, suicides, and other external causes—precisely when legal purchase becomes possible. That discontinuity implies that shifting the threshold from 21 to 18 would move the mortality increase earlier, raising deaths among 18- to 20-year-olds rather than leaving the total roughly unchanged.

Other factors (safer cars, seat-belt laws, broader anti-drunk-driving efforts) have also reduced fatalities, and the exact number of lives saved each year is debated. Those caveats affect the magnitude, not the direction: the weight of the evidence indicates fewer young people die under a drinking age of 21 than would die under a drinking age of 18.

CONFIDENCE: 82

No. The claim that seed oils (soybean, canola, sunflower, corn, and similar oils) are a major driver of obesity or chronic disease is not supported by the balance of human evidence.

These oils are mostly unsaturated fat, especially linoleic acid (an omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid). When they replace saturated fat, randomized trials and large cohort studies generally show lower LDL cholesterol and lower cardiovascular risk, not higher. Major reviews used by cardiology groups reach that conclusion; they do not treat ordinary dietary linoleic acid as a primary cause of heart disease.

The inflammation argument is overstated. Linoleic acid can be converted toward arachidonic acid, but in people eating typical amounts that conversion is limited, and controlled studies do not show a consistent rise in inflammatory markers. Some find neutral or slightly lower markers. A high omega-6 to omega-3 ratio is a weaker target than simply eating enough omega-3s (fish, or ALA from foods such as canola, flax, or walnuts) and not overeating overall.

- Very high intakes of any refined fat, inside a junk-food pattern, are a poor idea.
